title: Global Payments faces industry pricing pressure
snippet: While analysts point to an increasingly competitive environment for the processor, the company is still trying to raise prices.
fullText:
Global Payments and other processors face an increasingly competitive market, with rising pricing pressures forcing some businesses in the ecosystem to consider consolidation.

Global Payments has touted increased merchant acceptance of its Genius point-of-sale services brand, but now it may be trying to force through price hikes in an increasingly competitive market.

The payments processing company is seeking to implement a new $699 annual fee for its merchant clients next month, according to a merchant consultant who posted a portion of a Global Payments letter on LinkedIn. 

“Worldpay, now part of Global Payments, is introducing a $699 annual fee, with the first charge hitting merchant statements this December. Yes, another one,” Merchant Cost Consulting Partner Matt Rej said in the LinkedIn post last week. “And this is on top of the other increases we've already seen from Worldpay this year.”

Rej questioned, and poked fun at, the reasoning Global Payments provided for the increase, pointing to the company’s letter saying: “Government and industry regulations have had a significant impact on system requirements in the payment processing industry.”

The Atlanta-based company didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Nonetheless, in its third-quarter earnings press release last week, the company acknowledged “increased competition in the markets in which we operate.”

Global Payments pricing moves come less than a year after it completed its $24.25 billion purchase of the merchant services company Worldpay, which could give the company stronger pricing power in the industry. In the third-quarter report, Global Payments reported that the Genius brand, which was launched last year, was placed at 65% more merchant locations, compared to the year-earlier period, and bookings more than doubled.   

As the Genius brand gains traction, the company is reportedly considering selling itself off to one of its largest shareholders, private equity firm GTCR, and the investment firm Clayton, Dubilier & Rice. GTCR is acquainted with Global Payments partly because it was one of the companies that sold it the Worldpay assets.

Any fee increases by POS service providers are increasingly met with pressure from younger financial technology companies building a presence in the market with newer technologies. As a result, some legacy companies that provide payments services to merchants, including behemoth Fiserv, the new entrant Shift4 and the Dutch company Adyen, are feeling a competitive crunch.

Point-of-sale services firm PayCompass said in September that it had merged with two other firms and the CEO at the merchant services provider Butter Payments said last month that the company had sold its assets to an unnamed buyer.

While analysts who follow Global Payments praised the company’s progress in integrating Worldpay into its operations and luring merchants to the Genius brand, they noted the increasingly competitive market. As such, price increases may be a tough sell, particularly as merchants face consumers stretched by inflationary pressures. 

Analysts at the investment firm William Blair raised concerns about Global Payments technology being capable of competing with new fintechs.

“While sales metrics appear strong, we argue Genius is simply not a competitive offering from a technology standpoint and will not become material enough to durably accelerate consolidated organic growth,” the analysts said in a Thursday note to their clients, acknowledging the brand’s third-quarter growth.

Other analysts who follow the company also pointed out the competitive intensity in the market in commenting on Global Payments results.

“The Payments industry is very competitive with both existing and emerging competition,” analysts for TD Cowen told clients in a note Thursday. “All of our companies face the risk of being unable to capture market share or having their business models become commoditized by newer entrants in the market. Additionally, our companies are levered to consumer spending and therefore are exposed to general economic conditions.”

Analysts who follow the company for the investment firm R.W. Baird called out the difficulties for raising prices at this time across the industry. “Pricing pressure is a constant threat, and new fintechs have become competitive threats as well,” analysts at the Baird Equity Research arm said in a Thursday note. 

A sale to private owners might relieve some of the pressure of operating in the publicly traded market, with its focus on quarterly reports. Still, the analysts at William Blair last week gave the deal less than a 50-50 chance of being completed, partly because of the debt that Global Payments has in the wake of its Worldpay deal.

In a prior Oct. 30 note focused exclusively on the reports of a potential Global Payments sale, the William Blair analysts said that some $22 billion of debt at the company “could be an impediment, especially in a rising rate environment.”

The William Blair analysts posited that they could be wrong about the chances of the sale. If they are, they forecast that other “debt-laden” publicly traded companies in the industry, including Shift4 Payments and Fiserv, “pressure to sell will ratchet up dramatically, setting up what could be the final wave of industry consolidation.”

FCA to explore quantum computing to tackle financial crime

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

A new initiative will bring together firms, quantum technology providers, and national research labs to explore practical applications of quantum computing.

  

            						

The FCA will bring together financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories to explore how quantum computing could help tackle financial crime.

The Quantum Experimentation Group, the first of its kind for a regulator, will initially explore how quantum machine learning could help detect money laundering and fraud. It will launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Participants will use an FCA synthetic dataset – artificially generated data – to help overcome a key barrier to testing: access to suitable data.

The group will help firms explore practical uses of quantum computing in financial services and share findings to guide future testing. It will also help the FCA understand the technology’s opportunities and limitations, barriers to experimentation and what these could mean for regulation.

Jessica Rusu, chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, said: 'We want to help firms explore where quantum could make a meaningful difference, and early experimentation is essential to understanding its potential in financial services. By bringing together firms, technology providers and researchers we can build readiness and identify practical applications for common industry challenges, starting with financial crime.'

The initiative builds on the FCA’s research into the long-term potential of quantum computing in financial services.

Financial services firms, quantum technology providers and national research laboratories can register their interest in joining the group by 31 December 2026.

Notes to editors

Read more about the Quantum Experimentation Group and how to register an interest in joining the group.

The FCA’s Quantum Experimentation Group will be the world’s first regulator-led quantum computing experimentation group.

The group will support organisations at different stages of their quantum journey, from those beginning to explore potential use cases to those already undertaking advanced experimentation.

As part of the initiative, the FCA will define problem statements and work alongside participants to build understanding of the opportunities, limitations and practical considerations associated with quantum technologies.

The initiative will complement wider activity across the UK’s quantum ecosystem by creating additional opportunities for collaborative experimentation and learning.

title: TotallyMoney Hits Six Million Users as Credit-Score Habits Drive Gains
snippet: The free credit app said one-in-ten UK adults have now used its service, with monthly checkers recording a 133% larger score improvement than The post TotallyMoney Hits Six Million Users as Credit-Score Habits Drive Gains appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
TotallyMoney, the free credit report and score app operated by Intelligent Lending Group, has reached six million registered users in the UK, a milestone the Manchester-based company marked on 21 October 2026. The figure represents roughly 11% of the UK adult population, based on mid-2025 ONS population data cited by the company.

The platform provides users with live access to their TransUnion credit score and report, alongside automated alerts when the score changes and personalised guidance on improving their credit standing. It also acts as a lead-generation channel for credit cards, loans and other retail financial products, a model common among UK credit-comparison and credit-health platforms.

What the engagement data shows

Nik Charalampous, CEO at TotallyMoney

TotallyMoney’s internal analysis of more than 7,000 customers who joined in September 2025 and were tracked through to July 2026 found that 45% of those who started with a “low” TransUnion score (below 556) improved their score within six months. Among the lowest-scoring segment, customers who entered with a score below 400, the proportion who improved was 86%.

Frequency of use correlated strongly with outcome. Customers who checked their report every month achieved a score increase 2.3 times, or 133%, larger on average than those who engaged less regularly. The company attributes this to habitual monitoring prompting behaviour changes: paying down balances, correcting errors on a report, or simply avoiding missed payments. The analysis is self-reported and conducted by TotallyMoney’s own data team rather than an independent third party, a caveat worth noting.

Chief executive Nik Charalampous described the milestone as the result of people taking active control of their financial situations, and pointed to the breadth of circumstances driving sign-ups, ranging from thin-file consumers without an established UK credit record to those rebuilding after financial difficulty or preparing for a major credit commitment such as a mortgage.

Market context and competitive landscape

The UK credit-health market has matured considerably since TotallyMoney launched its free credit report service in 2017. Credit Karma, Experian‘s consumer app, ClearScore and MoneySuperMarket‘s credit tools compete for similar audiences, and all operate on variants of the same freemium model: offer free credit monitoring, monetise through matched product recommendations. The competitive advantage tends to sit in data depth, matching accuracy and the quality of the personalisation engine rather than in the report itself, since TransUnion, Equifax and Experian data is accessible across platforms.

For lenders, the segment matters because users who actively monitor their credit tend to be better-informed borrowers, and platforms that can demonstrate measurable score improvement have a stronger commercial proposition when negotiating referral or white-label arrangements with credit providers. TotallyMoney’s six-million-user figure positions it as a credible data asset within the Intelligent Lending Group portfolio alongside Binq, CredAbility, Ocean and Luv Cars.

The UK’s financial inclusion agenda adds a policy dimension. The FCA has placed increased emphasis on consumer understanding of credit and the fair treatment of customers in financial difficulty. Platforms that can show measurable credit-score improvement among thin-file or recovering borrowers align with that agenda, even if they sit outside the FCA’s direct regulatory perimeter as credit brokers rather than lenders. As open finance obligations develop under the broader Data and Smart Data Bill framework, credit-health apps will also be positioned to ingest a richer data set, which could deepen the personalisation that drives the engagement numbers cited here.

title: Standard Chartered Acquires Zodia Custody in Digital Assets Push
snippet: Standard Chartered has signed definitive agreements to buy 100% of Zodia Custody, consolidating its institutional digital asset custody operations globally. The post Standard Chartered Acquires Zodia Custody in Digital Assets Push appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Standard Chartered has entered into definitive agreements to acquire Zodia Custody, the institutional digital asset custodian it helped establish through its SC Ventures innovation arm. The transaction, announced on 21 October 2026, will see Standard Chartered I H Limited acquire 100% of Zodia Custody Limited, the parent of regulated operating entities spanning Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, the United Arab Emirates and Luxembourg. Completion remains subject to regulatory approvals and customary closing conditions.

Once integrated, Zodia Custody’s regulated business will sit inside Standard Chartered’s Securities Services division alongside its existing digital asset custody activities in the UAE and Luxembourg. The bank says the combination is intended to create a unified offering that covers both traditional and digital asset securities for institutional clients, removing the operational separation that has existed between the two lines.

The carve-out: Zodia Solutions

Ying Ying Tan, global head of securities services and digital assets at Standard Chartered

A notable structural feature of the deal is the concurrent separation of Zodia Custody’s software and professional services arm. That business will be transferred to a newly established entity, Zodia Solutions, housed under SC Ventures rather than absorbed into the bank’s core. Zodia Solutions will continue to provide bank-grade custody infrastructure to financial institutions, including Standard Chartered itself.

A consortium of bank investors will support Zodia Solutions, including NAB Ventures, Northern Trust Corporation, SBI Ventures, Further Ventures (Q Studio), Emirates NBD, Investcorp’s Zodia Investments, and SC Ventures. The structure effectively preserves the vendor relationship with third-party institutions while giving Standard Chartered full ownership of the regulated custody entity. No financial terms for either the acquisition or the capitalisation of Zodia Solutions were disclosed.

Ying Ying Tan, global head of securities services and digital assets at Standard Chartered, said the deal “deepens our digital asset custody portfolio and reinforces our position as a leading provider of digital asset services globally, supported by the depth, breadth and global connectivity of an international cross-border bank.”

Market and regulatory context

Richard Clark, CEO at Zodia Custody

The acquisition reflects a broader consolidation trend in institutional digital asset custody. As regulators in major jurisdictions have moved to clarify the treatment of crypto assets held on behalf of clients, the custody layer has become a strategic priority for tier-one banks rather than a speculative adjacency. In the EU, MiCA’s requirements for crypto-asset service provider authorisation have accelerated demand for licensed custodians with established banking relationships. In Asia, Hong Kong’s VASP licensing regime and Singapore’s MAS framework have similarly pushed institutional clients towards regulated, bank-affiliated counterparties.

Standard Chartered’s move brings regulated custody licences across five jurisdictions into a single ownership structure, which is a meaningful regulatory footprint. Few custodians of any type can offer that breadth under one bank’s balance sheet, and the combination with an established securities services business creates a cross-sell opportunity into the bank’s existing institutional client base.

Competitors in the institutional custody space include Anchorage Digital, Copper and Coinbase Custody at the specialist end, as well as BNY Mellon and Citigroup, which have been building digital asset custody capabilities within their own securities services businesses. The Standard Chartered and Zodia Solutions model, where the software platform remains available to third-party banks, is an attempt to capture infrastructure revenue beyond the bank’s own custody clients.

Richard Clark, chief executive of Zodia Custody, noted that “custody is increasingly becoming part of the global banking landscape” as institutional adoption accelerates. The next markers to watch are which jurisdictions grant regulatory approval first and how quickly the combined custody offering is brought to market for Securities Services clients.

title: California DFPI Opposes SEC Crypto Rule Over State Oversight Risk
snippet: California's financial regulator has filed a formal comment letter against an SEC proposal it says would strip states of authority to screen digital asset The post California DFPI Opposes SEC Crypto Rule Over State Oversight Risk appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
California’s Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) has formally opposed a Trump administration Securities and Exchange Commission proposal, filing a public comment letter arguing that the rule, labelled “Regulation Crypto Assets,” would effectively dismantle the state’s ability to review and block high-risk digital asset securities offerings before they reach investors.

KC Mohseni, Commissioner at Califronia’s DFPI

The release number is SEC Release No. 33-11434. The DFPI’s objection, signed by Commissioner KC Mohseni, was submitted on 20 October 2026.

The regulatory dispute

At its core, the dispute is about the boundary between federal and state securities law. Under existing US securities law, certain exempt offerings must still clear state-level “blue sky” review, a process California uses to screen offerings for fraud risk before they are marketed to residents. The SEC’s proposed rule, in the DFPI’s reading, would create a federal preemption pathway for crypto asset offerings, removing that state review stage.

The DFPI argues that the practical consequence would be a meaningful reduction in the number of fraudulent offerings intercepted before harm occurs. Commissioner Mohseni said California would not accept “a coordinated attempt by federal regulators to override state authority and protections while stepping back from the oversight they are supposed to provide.” California Business and Consumer Services Secretary Rohit Chopra characterised the SEC move as an attempt to “muzzle state oversight” at the same time as federal enforcement of investment fraud rules is being curtailed.

The DFPI also raised a wider concern: it said the same preemption logic, once established for digital assets, could be extended to other investment categories, weakening state protections beyond the crypto sector.

Market context and the fraud backdrop

The scale of the problem the DFPI is trying to police is not trivial. The FBI‘s Internet Crime Complaint Center reported record losses of $11.3 billion from crypto-related scams in 2025. California’s own Crypto Scam Tracker added nearly 200 new entries in the period, a year-on-year increase of approximately 30 per cent. Those figures provide the DFPI with a concrete evidential basis for its opposition, beyond the jurisdictional argument.

The release also pointed to a recent state enforcement action as an illustration of active state-level oversight: the DFPI ordered Fire Suppression Innovations Inc. to halt illegal stock sales, return $2.9 million to investors and pay $785,500 in fines after the company was found to have fabricated a $5 billion buyout, concealed personal expenditure and operated a Ponzi-like structure.

The broader regulatory read-across is significant for the digital assets sector globally. In the US, the OCC, SEC and CFTC have each been recalibrating their jurisdictional positions on crypto assets since early 2025, and the question of federal preemption versus state-level oversight has become a live fault line. The DFPI’s intervention is the latest in a series of state-level pushbacks against federal rule-making that states argue reduces investor protection while simultaneously reducing federal enforcement activity. Similar tensions are visible in the EU context, where MiCA’s uniformity across member states was partly designed to prevent equivalent regulatory fragmentation, though it raises different debates about the adequacy of a single supervisory tier for novel instruments.

For compliance officers and digital asset issuers operating across US states, the outcome of this rulemaking matters practically. If the SEC proceeds and the preemption argument holds, blue sky review for certain digital asset offerings would fall away in states like California. If the states successfully contest the rule, the current patchwork of state-by-state review requirements would remain, with attendant compliance costs for issuers seeking to raise capital from retail investors.

title: Emirates Islamic Posts AED 3.3bn Operating Profit in Nine-Month Results
snippet: The UAE Islamic bank grew total income 6% year-on-year to AED 4.7bn, with customer financing up 14.4% and deposits rising 13 The post Emirates Islamic Posts AED 3.3bn Operating Profit in Nine-Month Results appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Emirates Islamic, the Islamic banking arm of Emirates NBD Group, has reported an operating profit of AED 3.3 billion for the first nine months of 2026, a 7% increase year-on-year. Net profit held broadly stable at AED 2.7 billion, supported by double-digit growth in both financing and deposits and a healthy net profit margin of 3%.

Total income reached AED 4.7 billion, up 6% on the same period a year earlier, with the bank attributing the improvement primarily to higher non-funded income. Operating expenses rose 5% to AED 1.4 billion, which management described as reflecting continued strategic investment. Impairment charges came in at AED 141 million.

Balance sheet and capital position

Farid AlMulla, chief executive officer at Emirates Islamic

The balance sheet expanded meaningfully over the nine-month period. Total assets grew 8.6% to AED 158.3 billion, while customer financing climbed 14.4% to AED 101.6 billion and customer deposits increased 13.4% to AED 115.8 billion. Current and savings account balances accounted for 63.2% of total deposits, a metric the bank flagged as evidence of a resilient and lower-cost funding mix.

Capital ratios remain well above minimum thresholds. The Common Equity Tier 1 ratio stood at 15.1% and the overall capital adequacy ratio at 16.2%, leaving meaningful headroom under Basel III requirements as applied by the UAE Central Bank. The financing-to-deposit ratio of 87.7% sits within management’s stated target range.

Credit quality metrics held steady. The non-performing financing ratio was 2.4%, covered at 151.5%, a coverage level that provides a material buffer against any deterioration in asset quality as rate conditions evolve across the Gulf.

Chief executive Farid AlMulla said the results reflected strength across all business segments. “Double-digit growth in both financing and deposits reflects the strength of our franchise and customers’ growing preference for Emirates Islamic, supported by market share gains across Retail, Corporate and SME banking,” he said.

The bank also disclosed an MoU with Dubai Chambers to provide Shariah-compliant banking services to members of the Dubai Chamber of Commerce, covering trade finance, cash management and corporate financing. The partnership is primarily distribution-oriented, giving Emirates Islamic access to a broad base of SME customers at a moment when business banking is a stated growth priority. The bank says it already serves more than 45,000 SMEs in the UAE.

Market context and regulatory read-across

Emirates Islamic operates in a competitive Islamic finance market in which several regional institutions, including Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank and Kuwait Finance House, are pursuing similar balance sheet growth strategies. The sector is being shaped by the UAE’s Islamic Finance and Halal Industry Strategy 2025 to 2031, which sets a policy framework for expanding Shariah-compliant financial products across both retail and wholesale segments.

The bank also highlighted its USD 500 million Sustainability-Linked Financing Sukuk, which received the “World’s Best Sukuk Deal” award at the Euromoney Islamic Finance Awards 2026. The bank describes it as the first sustainability-linked sukuk of its kind globally, a claim that reflects the early-stage nature of ESG integration in Islamic capital markets. Sukuk structures are attracting growing regulatory attention in the context of the UAE’s broader sustainable finance agenda, and deals of this type are likely to face increasing disclosure expectations as green and sustainability-linked bond frameworks are tightened internationally.

Looking ahead, the key variables to watch are the trajectory of non-funded income as interest rate dynamics in the Gulf shift, the pace at which the bank converts its SME pipeline into recurring fee revenue, and the timeline for further licence or product developments under the national Islamic finance strategy.

title: Air India and Standard Chartered Link Loyalty with Wealth Management
snippet: The airline and the bank will offer affluent Global Indians reciprocal travel status and cross-border wealth services across Singapore and the UAE. The post Air India and Standard Chartered Link Loyalty with Wealth Management appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Air India and Standard Chartered have announced a partnership linking the airline’s redesigned Maharaja Club loyalty programme with the bank’s international wealth management services, initially targeting affluent Indian diaspora customers in Singapore and the UAE.

Under the arrangement, eligible Standard Chartered clients who meet the bank’s affluent-tier criteria will receive Maharaja Club Gold or Silver status, unlocking benefits including priority boarding, additional baggage allowance, airport lounge access, upgrade vouchers and bonus Maharaja Points. Gold tier members also inherit Star Alliance Gold status, granting access to more than 1,000 lounges across 25 member airlines beyond Air India itself.

The flow runs in both directions. Air India customers who qualify under Standard Chartered’s eligibility criteria can access the bank’s wealth centres in Singapore and the UAE, receiving dedicated relationship management, market outlook briefings from the bank’s Chief Investment Office, and tailored solutions pitched at cross-border financial planning.

The proposition

Rajesh Kannan, head of wealth and retail banking for UAE and Jersey and head of global Indian clients at Standard Chartered, said the partnership was designed for customers “whose lives, business and ambitions increasingly span borders,” framing the deal as a convergence of Air India’s expanding route network with the bank’s international footprint across 55 markets.

Air India’s chief commercial officer, Nipun Aggarwal, positioned the tie-up as part of the airline’s broader transformation under the Vihaan.AI programme, which has included orders for 600 new aircraft since the carrier returned to Tata Sons ownership in 2022. The Maharaja Club itself was redesigned in 2024, gaining a simplified tier structure and, according to the airline, adding millions of new members. The programme now covers earn-and-redeem across 104 destinations and partnerships with more than 100 brands across hospitality, retail, lifestyle and financial services.

The proposition is expected to be available within the coming weeks. The two companies did not disclose the commercial terms of the arrangement, including any revenue-share structure, minimum customer thresholds or marketing commitments.

Market context

The combination of airline loyalty status and private or affluent banking is not new. Several international banks have structured similar tie-ups, particularly in markets where high-net-worth and upper-mass-affluent customers are frequent long-haul travellers. What is less common is an airline that is simultaneously undergoing a large-scale fleet and service transformation using the loyalty programme as a distribution channel for financial services acquisition, rather than as a retention tool alone.

The Global Indian segment is a genuinely significant addressable market. The Indian diaspora in Singapore and the UAE includes a substantial share of senior executives, entrepreneurs and investors who hold assets across multiple jurisdictions and carry complex cross-border banking needs. Standard Chartered has built its retail and wealth strategy around precisely this demographic for several years, and the airline partnership adds a tangible, immediate benefit at the point of customer acquisition.

From a regulatory standpoint, the wealth management component sits within Standard Chartered’s existing licences in Singapore and the UAE. The UAE’s financial services environment, overseen by the DFSA in the Dubai International Financial Centre and the ADGM in Abu Dhabi, has seen growing competition for affluent cross-border clients, with several international banks expanding their Gulf presence to serve the same diaspora segment. The partnership does not appear to require new regulatory approvals beyond those the bank already holds.

The near-term test will be uptake rates and whether the status offer is sufficient to prompt actual account opening rather than casual interest from existing Air India passengers.

Quantum computing will bring significant opportunities to the UK financial sector, but firms need to act now to prepare for a world where a viable hostile quantum computer could break today’s widely used cryptography standards.

The financial sector depends on secure information and communication. Cryptography – of which encryption is just one part – helps firms protect their clients’ data, verify who they are dealing with, and maintain trust in their systems.

Sufficiently powerful quantum computers pose a real threat to that security. Without trustworthy cryptography, consumers would face fraud, firms would suffer operational disruption, and the integrity of financial transactions and markets would be put at risk.

That’s why we are talking to firms about preparing for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) now. We don’t know for certain when a viable quantum computer will emerge, but the coming years will likely see the technology advance at a rapid pace.

Preparing for this new world requires firms to understand where and how they use cryptography and to be able to migrate all hardware and software to PQC, while managing operational risks.

Realistically, for most firms, this will require significant time, investment and effort.

What firms need to do now

So, what kind of timescale are we talking about? The National Centre for Cyber Security (NCSC) recommends 3 key milestones:

By 2028, firms complete a PQC migration plan.

By 2031, firms carry out high-priority migration activities.

By 2035, firms have migrated all systems, services and products to PQC.

Firms should not wait for these milestones before acting and where it is safe to do so, they should seek to be ready sooner. In line with NCSC guidance, we expect firms to act now to: 

Have a thorough and accurate understanding of the cryptography in place across systems and information.

Set clear, achievable, safe and risk-based migration objectives..

Implement migration plans and monitor, test and validate the changes, adjusting them where necessary.

Senior managers should ensure that their firms allocate enough time, investment and resources to manage PQC migration safely and meet the relevant deadlines. Failed change projects accounted for around a fifth of all incidents reported to us in 2025.

How we are supporting firms

We are trialling a new supervisory self-assessment tool with an initial sample of firms and intend to extend it to other firms in due course. This will help firms assess the maturity of their plans and help us understand the industry’s preparedness for PQC migration.

This trial will also help us identify common challenges and examples of good practice, which we intend to share with the sector.

We shared relevant insights from firms in April 2026 and will continue to engage with the industry through our Cyber Coordination Groups (CCGs), the Cross Market Operational Resilience Group (CMORG), and trade bodies and associations.

We will also consult on cyber resilience guidance for firms, including our expectations for how firms should address PQC risks through their cryptographic controls.

You can find more information:

NCSC, Timelines for migration to post-quantum cryptography 

G7 Cyber Expert Group, Statement on advancing a coordinated roadmap for the transition to post-quantum cryptography in the financial sector 

CMORG, Guidance for post-quantum cryptography

title: Europe’s single market still has borders
snippet: how a business can localise its financial operations in a new market, without rebuilding them every time. The post Europe’s single market still has borders appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
With international expansion coming earlier and earlier in a business’ growth strategy, Vivien Cheung, Senior Director of Strategic Banking Partnerships at Airwallex, explains how a business can localise its financial operations in a new market, without rebuilding them every time. 

The expansion plan is ready: pricing, hiring, a launch date. Then the first payment doesn’t arrive.

The payer’s system had taken one look at the account details and flagged them with an error. That’s where the borders turn up. Not at a checkpoint, but in a payment system that doesn’t recognise the account.

Europe may appear like one market to a multinational business planning its next move, and it’s also why the gaps are so easy to miss. Banking arrangements, payment habits and regulators’ expectations still differ country by country. A failed payment is only the visible symptom, behind it sit accounts, entities and currencies that don’t necessarily line up.

I’ve supported customers through various market launches, and this pattern is consistent. Businesses spend months perfecting their entry and almost no time on what happens next. The EU’s single market opens the door to European trade, but it doesn’t do the operational work. As AI agents take on more of the finance function, that gap will only widen.

Localising to reuse not rebuild

The finance stack needs to ensure customers can pay the way they expect, suppliers can be paid without friction, and finance teams can see it all in one place.

In the Netherlands, an Airwallex customer can have a local Dutch IBAN, access to SEPA credit transfers, instant payments and direct debits, payment through iDEAL or Wero, a locally issued card and one view across every entity and currency. Each removes a small point of friction. Together, they separate a business that looks local from one that only sells there. Local regulation matters just as much. Every country has its own regulator with its own expectations, and it’s far better to learn them before you arrive than after. But tackle each one in isolation and localisation becomes fragmentation, with every country ending up as its own product.

A small business doesn’t need to become a specialist in local banking and regulation just because it scaled internationally. The goal instead should be to work from a core system that can be reused in each new market, then decide deliberately where to localise on top of it.

Connected systems are a growth decision

Every new market can add another account, another provider, and another set of records. When those systems don’t talk to each other, finance teams reconcile manually, and a failure can take days to trace back to its source. IMF research notes that Europe’s retail payments systems remain largely segmented even within national borders, which can impede small firms’ ability to scale beyond their home market.

At Airwallex, we chose to build our own infrastructure, acquiring 85+ licenses over a decade, which our founder and CEO, Jack Zhang, calls the ‘Path of Max Resistance’. It may have taken us longer to start, but it made sense in the long-run to build the core foundations that run global payments. Businesses want their financial operations to run on one system, with money moving reliably and instantly, which is much harder to guarantee across a chain of providers’ and their fragmented systems.

Now that our core infrastructure rails are in place, we are adding the global intelligence layer on top. The focus for each new market is about localising, not rebuilding. Localising doesn’t mean going it alone: the right partners still give us the local reach and the trust that every new market demands.

Readiness is organisational

The technology stack is the obvious place to start when asking whether you’re ready for the next market. Experience has taught me to check something less exciting: whether your teams are aligned behind one goal and know who is accountable for delivering it.

Expansion is one of the most cross-functional things a company will do. Product, finance, legal, compliance and operations all depend on each other, and one blocked workstream soon holds up three others. Three questions are worth stress-testing before launch. Does the end-to-end experience feel like one product? Is it clear what is strategically important to control? And who can make the final call when workstreams collide?

One of my biggest learnings is to invest in project management before it’s needed, and to give the team the mandate and seniority to drive decisions, not just track them. A ten-person business won’t have a project team, but it can name one person with that authority and a clear route to escalate. Each launch should leave behind processes the next one can reuse.

Agents raise the stakes

AI agents don’t change the fundamentals of expansion, they raise the stakes. When payments and financial decisions happen at agentic speed, the gaps a human team could work around become failures. A finance manager can step in and fix a problem manually, but an agent can’t. If your payments depend on several third parties, it inherits every handoff, delay, and dependency.

Knowing who controls the core infrastructure, such as how money moves and how risk and compliance are managed, is critical. It decides whether or not agents run on one consistent system. The model that works is one where people set the objectives and rules, and agents act within them. These foundations will determine if a business can keep up.

There is a significant opportunity for small businesses as agents make it easier to operate internationally, and I’m confident the businesses that win will be the ones whose infrastructure was built to support that from the start. At Airwallex, our goal is to give small businesses access to the sophisticated infrastructure of a global company, wherever their home market or whatever their headcount.

The expansion plan is the easy part. What decides whether that first payment arrives is the infrastructure underneath it.

title: BNPL for rent seeks a market
snippet: A new crop of fintechs is exploring growth opportunities in pay-later lending for monthly rent payments as inflation pinches consumers.
fullText:
Pay-later loans are increasingly available for monthly housing payments as financial technology companies seek growth by responding to consumers’ affordability struggles.

While the buy now, pay later market has traditionally focused on providing consumers with financing at retail merchants for discretionary items, a newer batch of companies sees profit potential in tailoring loans to rental payments and other monthly bills such as utilities, medical care and telephone service.

A variety of players have moved into the pay-later rental arena in recent years, aiming to fill financial gaps between consumers’ monthly rents and their incomes, as the increases in the former outpace the latter.

Ariel Nelson

Permission granted by National Consumer Law Center

The rise of these businesses is “really revealing in what they say about the state of affordability around life essentials,” said Ariel Nelson, a senior attorney with the National Consumer Law Center. “These products are really appealing because people are desperate.”

Companies seeking to develop a market in the rental area include RealPage, an apartment management software firm, which last year bought Livble, a startup that offers renters flexible payment options. Another is New York-based Flexible Finance, known as Flex, which lets consumers split their rent, mortgage or other monthly bill payments. 

A third rent-focused fintech is Bilt Technologies, which offers a payments and loyalty program aimed at attracting rent and mortgage payments to its co-branded credit cards. In addition to points for rent and everyday spending on its cards, New York-based Bilt issues points for homeowners’ association and condominium fee payments.

Bilt cardholders can transfer the points to 18 airline and seven hotel loyalty partner programs to redeem for flights and hotel stays. The points can also be redeemed at merchants such as Amazon.com and Lyft.

Consumer advocates contend that pay-later products aimed at rent and medical care can exacerbate financial strains for economically vulnerable people and lead to a stacking of their debt.

“As the price of shelter has shot up, a new breed of predatory creditors has emerged aiming to turn this emergency into profit,” advocacy group Protect Borrowers said in a February report on the rent now, pay later industry. “Beneath the surface, these products are united in being little more than a repackaging of an age-old debt trap: payday loans.”

About 109 million Americans have a monthly rental payment, according to Protect Borrowers, a Washington-based nonprofit that lobbies and litigates on consumer debt issues. The group was formed in 2018 as the Student Borrower Protection Center by former officials of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. 

Pay-later options allow renters to avoid being late on their rent, avoiding landlords’ late fees and revolving credit card interest rates that can reach 30% or more, Zahir Khoja, RealPage’s chief fintech officer, said in an interview last month. The average late fee is $85, he said.

“It’s not that you can’t pay your rent,” he said of tenant customers that select pay-later plans. “You may not be able to pay your rent on January 1st, and so you need some time in the month of January to be able to do it. It’s much better than paying a late fee or revolving at 29.9 (percent) on credit.”

Another BNPL provider, Sydney-based Zip, offers a bill-payment service to split monthly bills such as insurance, utilities and mobile phone. The company is also exploring a new rent-focused service for the U.S. market. 

Many “everyday Americans” are challenged by a misalignment between the timing of their income and bills, Zip’s former U.S. CEO, Joe Heck, told analysts on the BNPL provider’s August earnings call. Heck left Zip last month, the company said in an Oct. 16 investor announcement.

“Most consumers are paid every two weeks, while bills like rent are generally due monthly,” Heck said. “That mismatch in timing of income and expenses creates large opportunities beyond BNPL,” he said, pointing to bill payments and the need for “income-smoothing” as other ways the services could be used. 

Shragie Lichtenstein

Permission granted by Flex

The U.S. monthly rent and bill market is a $2 trillion addressable opportunity, compared to $160 billion for the retail BNPL market, Zip said in its investor presentation.

“I do think that this is a trend, both for rent and in general consumer essentials, that’s likely to continue,” Flex co-founder and CEO Shragie Lichtenstein said in an interview Oct. 8. 

Competing payment plans

RealPage, which is based in suburban Dallas, sells property-management software and rent payment financing services. The company offers both Livble and Flex via its app for residents and property managers or owners. 

Despite its Livble ownership, RealPage promotes both brands with its property owner customers, Khoja said. “We tell them ‘Hey, it’s Pepsi (or) Coke. Let the customer decide which one works for them.’”

Flex is a subscription service for tenants that collects a percentage of the rent as a payment for the service, he said Oct. 18, during an interview at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas. “Whereas ours (Livble) is just a flat fee, so it’s different – whatever works for you better as the resident.”

Another difference is that Flex offers credit cards as a payment method, while Livble accepts only ACH, said Khoja, who joined RealPage in March. 

Livble charges customers a fee for each payment they make, eschewing recurring monthly membership or subscription fees. Livble’s typical payment fee is $30 to $35 but are “nuanced by state,” which is why they’re not posted on the company’s website, a RealPage spokesperson said last week in an email. A resident using Livble, “will always know the fee before it’s final,” the spokesperson said. The company didn’t immediately respond to a question about how it presents its fees to customers. 

“We don’t want you to get into perpetual debt,” Khoja said. “Our goal is to actually help you go up the financial-inclusion ladder, where you’re now able to stand on your own two feet and do things without revolving credit at such high rates or taking third-party loans that you can’t repay.”

A playground at an apartment complex in Irving, Texas, near Dallas.

Getty Images

Two years ago, the Justice Department and eight states filed an antitrust lawsuit alleging that RealPage helped apartment owners collude to fix rental prices. The lawsuit said that the company’s pricing software used nonpublic, sensitive data collected from apartment owners to develop rental rate recommendations in various markets and keep rents higher than they would have been in a competitive market.

The company and government settled the case last year, with RealPage agreeing to stop using sensitive information from landlords to determine the rental prices that it suggested through its software. The company did not admit or deny wrongdoing or face a financial penalty as part of the agreement. Several antitrust lawsuits filed by states and private plaintiffs continue. Private equity firm Thoma Bravo acquired RealPage in 2021. 

Another rent-payment focused startup, New York-based Esusu, has partnered with BNPL provider Affirm Holdings to allow renters to split their rent into two equal payments. The Esusu program remains an “early-stage pilot” in testing and consists only of evenly split rent payments, with no fees or interest, an Affirm spokesperson said last month in an email.

Esusu charges a $59 membership fee, paid monthly or annually, depending on whether a tenant’s apartment property is part of the company’s network. The company also has a “split pay” program allowing renters to pay 60% of their rent upfront and divide the remainder into two or three payments. Esusu did not respond to a message seeking comment on its business model. 

Determining the costs of these rent-payment programs “can be confusing,” said Nelson, the NCLC attorney, noting that such information is often buried deep within user terms and conditions.

“I cannot for the life of me figure out how much they cost,” she said of having looked around different pay-later providers’ websites for pricing information. “And that’s also a problem.”

Scattered regulatory oversight

Pay-later lending has had little oversight at the federal level. Several states – including Illinois, New York and Oregon – have formulated rules to regulate the industry as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has contracted during the Trump administration. 

In June, U.S. Rep. Daniel Goldman, a Democrat from New York City, introduced a bill to apply the federal Truth in Lending Act to BNPL loans, effectively regulating them as credit cards. The measure hasn’t moved beyond the House Financial Services Committee, according to Congress’ website.

BNPL “users have been left with no federal protections,” Goldman said in a press release announcing his bill, referring to the CFPB’s decision to retreat last year from a 2024 decision to regulate pay-later loans much like credit cards.

Another bill, filed by Sen. Jack Reed, a Rhode Island Democrat, would amend the Truth in Lending law, which dates to the late 1960s, and the 2010 Consumer Financial Protection Act to apply new oversight and consumer protections. Reed’s legislation, filed late last year, has attracted four Democratic co-sponsors and a companion bill in the House, but no Republican sponsors, according to Congress.gov.

Lichtenstein, the Flex CEO, said that one challenge facing the RNPL industry is that these products “don’t fit into a clean box” neatly for regulators to evaluate what they are and how they work.

“The more you don’t fit into a clean box, the more regulatory scrutiny it draws,” he said. “We have tried our best to fit into a relatively clean box,” he said, adding that the company has “internal guardrails” to help it evaluate “the many, many gray areas that can exist for consumer fintech.”

However, he added, pay-later services for rent differ from other financial services, often “embedded” with the rent payment and with different pricing models. 

The RNPL industry doesn’t currently have a “uniform set of standards” from regulators under which to operate, Lichtenstein said, which can lead to different practices among the various players. “Continued clarity on the right way to do things would be welcome by us,” he said.

Risks for renters?

Beyond high fees and the potential for debt accumulation, rent-payment services pose “a significant risk” to borrowers because lenders often link directly to consumers’ bank accounts and offer “disastrously poor customer service” in addressing errors or other account issues, according to the Protect Borrowers report. 

Their growth is also likely to lead to further regulatory scrutiny, with at least one state, New York, being encouraged by the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection to apply its BNPL rules expansively to other providers in adjacent verticals. 

Pay-later services are marketed by lenders “who claim that these loans can ease the housing affordability or healthcare accessibility crisis,” Commissioner Samuel A.A. Levine of the New York City DCWP wrote in September in a letter to New York state financial regulators. “However, in both cases, these products fail to address the underlying problems and result only in consumers facing new and compounding risks.”

Among various recommendations to the state’s Department of Financial Services, Levine urged regulators to include “all forms of BNPL products” in its pending rules for such lenders, including those that offer rent payment services.

“The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

Ariel Nelson

National Consumer Law Center

Esusu raised $50 million last December. Its platform covers about 5 million rental units, with 12 million people, according to the company’s press release. The company also offers a rent-payment reporting service to help renters build their credit scores. 

Esusu says on its website that its credit services are needed because two-thirds of Americans “live paycheck to paycheck” and that about “30% of lower-income households spend 95% or more of their income on basic necessities like housing, food and utilities.”

Affirm doesn’t allow a consumer to borrow further if they have an outstanding balance from the prior month, Affirm’s vice president of government relations, John Pitts, wrote in a February blog post in response to the Protect Borrowers report, seeking to highlight differences between Affirm and others in the rent market.

“Being financially blindsided by hidden fees and/or still paying January’s rent in March is not solving affordability, it’s stacking debt,” Pitts wrote. “That’s why our products are structurally different.”

Regulators are beginning to “get educated in this space, and they're asking the right questions to provide the consumer protection around it,” said RealPage’s Khoja. Officials in states with the largest numbers of renters – California, Florida, New York and Texas – are among those gathering information about how RNPL firms work, he said.

However, the field of pay later for rent is nascent and state officials are still “catching up” with its growth, said Nelson, the consumer attorney.

“You’re talking about people who are doing whatever it takes to keep a roof over their head,” she said. “This isn’t like I couldn’t pay for an expensive pair of shoes – you could literally be homeless. The stakes are really high, so I think we need to be extremely cautious about how we handle products in this space.”

title: Signicat Names TÜV Austria Sole CAB for eIDAS 2.0 Compliance
snippet: Signicat is consolidating its eIDAS audits under a single conformity assessment body, replacing a five-CAB structure built up through acquisitions. The post Signicat Names TÜV Austria Sole CAB for eIDAS 2.0 Compliance appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Signicat, the Norwegian digital identity provider, has appointed TÜV Austria as its sole Conformity Assessment Body (CAB) for all eIDAS-related audits, replacing a fragmented arrangement in which five separate CABs assessed different parts of its business. The consolidation, announced on 20 October 2026, is a direct consequence of the company’s M&A-driven expansion and the growing regulatory demands of eIDAS 2.0.

The company’s acquisition trail had left it with compliance assessments spread across multiple bodies in different European jurisdictions. That structure added administrative overhead and made it harder for customers in regulated sectors, primarily banking, insurance and financial services, to get a coherent picture of Signicat’s compliance posture across its full service catalogue.

Why a single CAB matters under eIDAS 2.0

The timing of the consolidation is not incidental. The revised eIDAS regulation, eIDAS 2.0, establishes the framework for the EU Digital Identity Wallet and places new conformity assessment obligations on trust service providers. Signicat is already a participant in several of the EU’s large-scale wallet pilots, including WE BUILD, Aptitude, NOBID and EWC. Operating under a single CAB simplifies the audit trail as wallet interoperability standards are formalised, and makes it easier to combine eIDAS assessments with adjacent certifications such as ISO 27001 and SOC 2.

Jon Ølnes, VP of digital Identity and regulation at Signicat, said the company ran a formal request-for-information process among its existing CABs before selecting TÜV Austria. “We decided to run an RFI among the CABs and TÜV Austria had the best solutions and services to consolidate the situation and for the changes ahead as EUDI Wallets are introduced across Europe.”

TÜV Austria already assessed Signicat’s identity proofing service, giving it an existing baseline of the company’s technical environment. The transition to single-CAB coverage will be phased to avoid gaps in continuous compliance, according to the company.

Market and regulatory context

The consolidation reflects a broader maturation dynamic in the European digital identity sector. The European Commission has targeted adoption of an EU Digital Identity Wallet by 80 per cent of EU citizens by 2030, a target that is driving commercial demand for verifiable trust services and pushing providers to demonstrate audit-grade compliance at scale. Juniper Research has estimated the global digital identity market will reach 80 billion dollars by the same year, though such long-range market sizing projections carry wide uncertainty.

For Signicat’s bank and fintech customers, the practical benefit is transparency. A single CAB produces a unified compliance view that aligns more naturally with how regulated financial institutions conduct their own third-party due diligence. Banks operating under the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act, which came into full effect in January 2025, face stricter obligations around the oversight of critical technology suppliers, and a cleaner audit structure from a supplier reduces friction in that process.

Signicat, backed by Nordic Capital since 2019, serves more than 20,000 customers across 45 countries and employs over 530 people in 15 European markets. The company’s positioning as a pan-European identity orchestration layer means the quality and legibility of its compliance architecture is a commercial differentiator, particularly as the EUDI Wallet rollout draws in public-sector and cross-border use cases where multiple national supervisory bodies will scrutinise the underlying trust infrastructure.

snippet: The bank aims to expand its reach to more customers by offering services via the NCR Atleos ATMs in Target stores.

The bank aims to expand its reach to more customers by offering services via the NCR Atleos ATMs in Target stores.

        

            

        Published Nov. 6, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                A Target store in Bridgehampton, NY. The retailer is part of a new partnership to add ATM services from First Citizens.

Dive Brief:

First Citizens Bank is partnering with NCR Atleos to offer surcharge-free access to services via ATMs located at some 2,000 Target stores, the bank said in a press release last month. As part of the agreement, the bank’s customers can use the ATMs at Target stores to withdraw cash, check their account balances and transfer funds to eligible linked accounts without paying a fee, according to the Oct. 19 release.

“The consumer banking experience needs to meet customers where they are through multiple channels, whether in-person or digitally enabled,” First Citizens Bank’s head of consumer banking, Michael Wilson, said in the release. 

Meanwhile, NCR Atleos CEO Tim Oliver said Wednesday that the company’s sale to Brink’s is progressing, with expected completion of the transaction by January.

Dive Insight:

For NCR Atleos, which became a standalone company three years ago, the partnership with First Citizens allows it to add new service providers to its roster. 

The company separated from its parent in late 2023, creating two publicly traded companies: NCR Voyix and NCR Atleos. While NCR Atleos offers ATMs and other interactive teller machines for payments and banking services, NCR Voyix offers point-of-sale hardware and related services to restaurant, retail and other merchants.

As NCR Atleos has grown its corporate clientele, including by working with American Express and PayNearMe in recent years, its self-service banking segment has bolstered revenue. The company reported third-quarter earnings results Wednesday that showed its self-service banking segment rose 3% to $2.17 billion for the first nine months of the year, faster than its overall business revenue growth, which increased 2% to $3.23 billion for the period, according to the earnings press release. 

“Our service-led growth initiatives and investment in product innovation are encouraging financial institutions and retailers to choose our differentiated and comprehensive offering to meet their evolving self-service needs,” Oliver said in August when the company reported second-quarter earnings. 

NCR’s partnership with First Citizens comes as the ATM provider prepares to be acquired. In February, the Brink’s Company agreed to buy NCR Atleos in a cash and stock transaction valued at about $6.6 billion. As part of the deal, Brink’s will also take on $2.6 billion in NCR Atleos debt, a press release on the transaction said. 

Regulators have yet to approve the deal. The Competition and Markets Authority in the U.K. said Brink’s acquisition of NCR Atleos could limit competition, according to a September report from the news outlet Reuters. Earlier this month, the Wall Street Journal reported Brink’s plans to sell some subsidiaries in a move aimed at assuaging U.K. concerns.

“We continue to make meaningful progress on regulatory approval processes across the multiple jurisdictions, and have significantly advanced the integration planning activities for the pending combination of Atleos and The Brink’s Company,” Oliver said in the release this week.

title: OpenSea Mobile Launches with Social Trading Feed and 25% Referral Fees
snippet: OpenSea has brought its mobile app out of beta, adding a cross-chain social trading layer and a permanent fee-sharing referral programme. The post OpenSea Mobile Launches with Social Trading Feed and 25% Referral Fees appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
OpenSea has taken its mobile application out of beta and made it available to all users on iOS and Android, framing the launch as a step toward making digital asset ownership and exploration accessible beyond the existing crypto-native audience.

The app aggregates portfolio holdings across multiple wallets and more than 25 blockchains, and routes trades across chains without requiring users to manually bridge assets between networks. New accounts can be created in under a minute using an email address alongside Apple Pay or Google Pay, with no seed phrase or exchange account required. Assets remain in users’ own wallets rather than custodied by the platform.

Signals: social trading on public data

Devin Finzer, co-founder and CEO at OpenSea

At the centre of the product is a social feed called Signals, which surfaces trading activity pulled from public blockchain data across multiple platforms rather than only OpenSea’s own order flow. The company says this means activity cannot be fabricated using screenshots, since every trade in the feed is verifiable on-chain. Users can attach a written note to any purchase, explaining their reasoning; that note travels with the trade data to all followers. The design attempts to distinguish the feature from copy-trading products that rely on a single platform’s user base, though the practical liquidity and quality of the signal stream will depend on how many active, high-quality traders the app can attract.

In beta, OpenSea reported that 76% of more than 56,000 sign-ups were active users, a retention figure the company cited as evidence of product-market fit. The cohort is small relative to the broader digital asset trading population, and the metric covers the beta period only.

The referral structure pays the inviting user 25% of the trading fees generated by anyone they bring in, for as long as that person trades. Referred users receive a permanent 10% discount on trading fees. Both benefits are ongoing rather than time-limited, which represents a more aggressive revenue-sharing model than most consumer crypto platforms have offered.

“OpenSea Mobile is that bet paying off,” said Devin Finzer, co-founder and chief executive of OpenSea. “We helped millions of people take their first step into digital ownership, and we built this app to help millions more.”

Market context and competitive read

OpenSea occupies a complicated position in the digital asset marketplace sector. The platform was founded in 2017 and became the dominant NFT marketplace during the 2021-2022 cycle, but faced significant competition from Blur, which captured market share among professional traders with zero-fee listings and token incentives. The shift toward token trading alongside collectibles in this latest product reflects a broader repositioning away from NFT-only activity toward a wider digital asset trading surface.

The aggregation model, pulling in trades from external platforms, is notable because it reduces OpenSea’s dependence on its own order book for social proof. However, it also raises questions around data permissions and whether competing platforms will seek to restrict access to their activity feeds over time.

The 25% fee-sharing referral sits inside a regulatory environment that is still evolving. In the UK and EU, referral arrangements in financial services are subject to inducement rules; the US Securities and Exchange Commission has taken an increasingly active interest in the classification of digital assets and the activities of trading platforms. Whether OpenSea’s referral programme triggers broker-dealer or financial promotion obligations in any jurisdiction was not addressed in the release. That question will be relevant to platform operators and compliance teams monitoring the sector.

The next milestones to watch are trading volume figures once the app moves beyond its beta cohort, and whether the cross-chain aggregation model sustains activity or concentrates on a handful of the supported chains in practice.

fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

Only through partnership can we deliver the system-wide response needed to protect market integrity. And that is the foundation necessary so innovation can flourish, productivity can rise and growth can endure.

The UK is incredibly well placed to harness the power of new technology. The existing strength of this sector gives us a genuine head start.

If we can harness technological progress – if we continue to lead – financial services can place the UK at the forefront of this new era of innovation.

As regulators, we are committed to creating the conditions for you to do that.

Together, we can build a future that the whole country will be proud of…
