title: FIS, Toast CFOs exit
snippet: The chief financial officers are leaving the payments players as the companies grapple with separate challenges.
fullText:
Fidelity National Information Services and Toast separately disclosed that their chief financial officers are exiting, as they also announced third-quarter earnings results. 

At FIS, which provides payments services to banking and capital markets clients, the company announced the departure of James Kehoe, with no further explanation. Alexandra “Alex” Brooks will step into the CFO post on an interim basis starting Thursday as the company begins a search for a permanent replacement, according to a Wednesday press release.

The CFO change at Jacksonville, Florida-based FIS landed as the company adjusted its financial forecasts due to unexpected changes in the outlook for recurring revenue, citing new factors that are dragging on that income.

The shifts were mainly related to changed expectations at some of its banking clients as those customers encounter implementation delays and, in some cases, work through acquisition activity, CEO Stephanie Ferris explained on a webcast with analysts Wednesday. The change is happening as some customers move from services with more traditional licenses to the company’s more updated subscription software services, she said.

“Over the course of the third quarter, we started to see some client-directed conversion delays, primarily in our larger client base, and some impacts from the timing around large bank consolidation,” Ferris said on the webcast.

FIS divests prepaid business

She also noted that the company would invest in technology and security to assist clients with implementations and to prioritize cyber work.

“These factors will weigh on our results in the fourth quarter in 2027, and we expect them to largely fade in 2028,” Ferris said. 

FIS also disclosed during the third-quarter report that it had sold what it referred to as a “non-core, prepaid asset” for $100 million. A spokesperson for the company didn’t immediately respond to requests for more information about the unit or the buyer.

Kehoe has been with FIS since August 2023, joining shortly after Ferris became CEO in January of that year. Together, they took the company through a $24.25 billion sale last year of its merchants services business Worldpay to Global Payments, and the $13.5 billion acquisition of a card issuer business from Global Payments.

FIS reported third-quarter adjusted net earnings rose 5.3% to $831 million as operating revenue climbed 29%, on an adjusted basis, to $3.37 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

At Toast, the digital payments processor said that its president and chief financial officer, Elena Gomez, will leave her posts at the end of the year. Michael Senno, who has served as Toast’s senior vice president of finance, will become CFO at that time, the company said.

Gomez, who has been at Toast since May 2021 and guided the company through its initial public offering that year, said in the company’s earnings press release that it’s time “to take a break before my next chapter.”

Toast CEO criticizes lawsuit

Meanwhile, during a webcast with analysts on Tuesday, Toast’s CEO, Aman Narang, continued to make a case for fighting a lawsuit brought by the Federal Trade Commission and states last week. The federal and state regulators alleged in their lawsuit that the company exacted “hidden fees” and “unauthorized charges” from both merchants and consumers. 

Narang defended the contracts Toast negotiates with every restaurant, and other merchants, to provide services in the business-to-business industry. 

The lawsuit turns on the Federal Trade Commission Act and the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, barring companies from misleading customers. The regulators said Toast made “false or misleading claims” regarding its subscription and financing services; failed to make required disclosures; didn’t provide simple ways for customers to cancel their subscription; and charged customers without their consent. 

“We are incredibly disappointed with the FTC's decision to file the suit,” Narang told analysts on the earnings webcast. “We've been engaged with them and cooperating with them really over the past year, and fundamentally believe their application of ROSCA is unprecedented for custom contracts in B2B.”

Narang posited that the enforcement action on that basis could impact the entire industry. “If ROSCA were to apply to B2B custom negotiated contracts in a B2B context, it would have huge implications for, really, the whole industry and business contracts in general,” Narang contended. “We have a lot of confidence in our business practices and are ready to defend ourselves.” 

Toast reported third-quarter net income rose 60% to $169 million as revenue increased 21% to $1.98 billion, according to the earnings press release.

The CFOs at both FIS and Toast said they’ll continue to work with the companies to transfer their duties to their successors.

title: How Barclays tucked into Samsung
snippet: Twenty-plus years into card co-brands, Barclays’ newest launch – a card integrated into Samsung’s digital wallet – offers both new challenges and opportunities.
fullText:
When Barclays entered the U.S. credit card market in 2004, it bet on a partnership model to set itself apart from competitors.

Twenty-two years later, a co-branded card originally started by the bank it acquired – the Frontier Airlines credit card, started by Juniper Bank in 2003 – is going strong. The partnership was extended in June, through 2037.

In July, Barclays launched another co-brand: the Samsung Galaxy Card, which integrates into the Samsung wallet when a customer is approved. (The card also has the potential to be its most far-reaching, as according to Samsung, one in seven people worldwide have a Galaxy phone. About 30% of U.S. smartphone users are Samsung Galaxy customers, according to Counterpoint Research.)

Launching this product was different than Barclays’ other co-brand products, in part because of an added “layer of coordination” between the bank and its partner, said Doug Villone, head of U.S. cards and partnerships at Barclays’ U.S. consumer bank. But the effort is paying off as adoption numbers are promising, according to Villone.

Villone explored this and other topics last month with Banking Dive at the Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

BANKING DIVE: You said adoption of the Samsung partnership was ahead of expectations. By what measure, and how far ahead?

DOUG VILLONE: Something you worry about when you launch a new co-brand, especially one with a very strong value proposition within the partner's properties, is that the card ends up being used to buy a phone [in Samsung’s case] but doesn't get used to buy your coffee.

We can’t share specific customer sign-up figures, but adoption has exceeded our internal business-case expectations. More than half of transactions are made through Samsung Pay, and most of those are outside Samsung’s own ecosystem. That suggests customers are using the card for everyday purchases, not just buying Samsung products. Overall, customer activity, spending and adoption have met or exceeded expectations so far.

Has customer feedback led to changes since launch?

We never viewed this as a “set it and forget it” product. We expect to add features and functionality over time. Currently, customers can complete about 70% of common servicing tasks in the Samsung Wallet, including making payments, viewing transactions and redeeming rewards. We’re not satisfied with that. 

There are still things that you might need to contact Barclays about, and we want to continue to make it so ultimately, you never have to leave the Samsung Wallet ecosystem to do that. We offer loans and deposits and other things to consumers in our other programs, and I can imagine a world where there would be more things that would be available to [Samsung Galaxy card] consumers as well – things like servicing chat, which we think would be a great add-on feature to what's already a very digital experience.

You’ve refreshed and updated the rewards proposition for a number of physical card partnerships this year. Is it harder or easier to update a wallet-based product than a traditional card?

It’s different. Samsung owns the experience because it’s sitting inside their wallet. There are a lot of capabilities we have for our other clients that we can make available to them, but the key difference is we have to work with Samsung’s development teams to ensure that we're exposing that – they're making sure this fits the Samsung experience that they're trying to create for their consumers. It creates a new layer of coordination.

As their operating system updates, we can bring things to life in a very seamless way to the consumer. So it’s almost a surprise when they have new features and functionality. But it does require a new layer of coordination, because it's something we're exposing to their property.

What are the next improvements or milestones you're working toward?

I firmly believe that if you have a product that sits in a wallet on your phone, you would want to be able to do everything you can from that. If you want to interact with us through a chat, you should be able to do most things through a chat. Think of every permutation of servicing over time – we would want to be able to do that.

What we launched was the most important things you could do: redeem rewards, do your transactions, pay your bill, lock your card, activate your card. But it’s not exhaustive. There are still things we want to enhance related to the servicing and the usage experience, as well as offering potentially other products in an integrated way. 

Your Frontier partnership isn’t the only long-term one. The co-branded card with Barnes & Noble is about 20 years old, and your partnership with JetBlue is 10. What makes a good refresh of a longstanding partnership?

It used to be that card co-brand card programs might refresh every five or 10 years. What we found is that you need to refresh products more often than that – in many cases, every three or four years. Sometimes the look and the feel of the product just needs to be modernized, but often it's the value proposition that may need to be refreshed. In some cases, consumers want a different product to meet them where they are.

For example, most co-brand products used to offer 1% to 3% in some kind of rewards currency. But now a lot of programs might offer you status; they might offer you lounge access. The consumer may want streaming credits, or they might want quadruple points at grocery stores. You have to adjust your product to meet what the consumer is looking for today, and that could be different than what they were looking for three or five years ago.

title: Cards draw customers, Marqeta CEO says
snippet: Companies have found there’s “almost nothing more engaging than a card,” CEO Mike Milotich said this week in an interview.
fullText:
Marqeta is attracting business from large companies that want to issue payment cards and other embedded services to deepen engagement with their customers, the fintech’s chief executive said in an interview this week.

Fortune 500 enterprises have recognized the power of card products due to the success and growth of fintechs’ services, CEO Mike Milotich said Wednesday in an interview, a day after the company reported third-quarter financial results and raised its profit outlook for 2026.

From the leader of a company that issues virtual and physical payments cards, his perspective is to be expected.

“People are realizing … that there’s almost nothing more engaging than a card product,” Milotich said. “A lot of these businesses are looking for engagement, they’re looking to drive their core business through a card product, getting you in their app, using their system, (and) their platform more.”

That trend directly benefits Marqeta, an Oakland, California-based fintech that also provides embedded finance services, including payment processing.

The average consumer uses a payment card 2.5 times each day, Milotich said, without providing details. “Besides maybe younger people checking their Instagram or something, there are very few things that people do that frequently,” he quipped.

A large company already has a significant customer base, which makes it easier “to insert a financial product” into its existing platforms, he said.

Marqeta enjoys “a long runway for growth” as the company “has barely scratched the surface (<1%) in a large addressable market of card-based money movement” totaling about $30 trillion, KBW analysts wrote Tuesday in a client note. 

However, the company sits at a point where growth from its top clients, including buy now, pay later companies, could decelerate and “new wins could take time to ramp,” they added.

Milotich, Marqeta’s former chief financial officer, was appointed to the top post on an interim basis in February 2025 and became CEO seven months later. The company has about 950 employees, a spokesperson said.

Marqeta’s larger customers also like the ability to have embedded solutions bundled, letting them avoid piecing together multiple vendors for each part of their planned offering, said Milotich, a former Visa executive who has also worked at PayPal Holdings and American Express.

“We can go to any customer and say, ‘If you want to do stablecoin, we have three options for you. We’ve already done the work and integrated, you can pull it through our APIs,’” he said. “That’s sort of where the business is moving.”

Last month, for example, Marqeta and the cryptocurrency platform Coinbase partnered on a stablecoin-backed payment card, allowing Marqeta customers to offer cards that apply stablecoin balances at merchants that accept cards.

The company has also announced a recent partnership with Google, for digital wallet tools aimed at children and parents. Last month, it worked with Square’s parent, Block, to introduce a business credit card for Square sellers – Marqeta’s first product on the American Express card network – as Block consolidated its Square cards.

For the third quarter, Marqeta reported net income of $115.4 million, compared to a $3.6 million loss in the same period last year, with total processing volume rising 29% to $126.5 billion. Revenue was $176.2 million, an 8% gain from the same quarter of 2025.

Block – the parent of Cash App, Square and Afterpay – accounted for 41% of Marqeta revenue in the quarter, down from 45% for the full year last year, according to regulatory filings, as that company has diversified its suppliers. Other Marqeta customers include Affirm Holdings, DoorDash, Uber Technologies and Western Union.

title: Shift4 signals caution
snippet: The payments processor is navigating weak demand for travel to Europe, and softer sales at its restaurant and hotel customers.
fullText:
Troubling economic conditions are continuing to vex Shift4 Payments, with the point-of-sale processor beset by travel weakness in Europe and reduced dining in the U.S.

Shift4 is navigating “a more challenging backdrop than we’ve seen in recent years,” CEO Taylor Lauber wrote in a shareholder letter accompanying the company’s third-quarter results on Thursday. The company cut its profit outlook and gross revenue target for the full year, with weak conditions expected to persist into 2027.

“Our business has been tested in many different ways this year, forcing us to adapt the business and make challenging calls,” Lauber said Thursday on a conference call with analysts to discuss the results. 

Fallout from the Iran conflict has bedeviled Shift4 in the European retail market, where it operates with Global Blue, the Swiss payments technology firm it acquired last year for $2.5 billion, including taking on $1 billion in debt. The Middle East and southeast Asia are significant sources of travel customers for Global Blue’s tax-free shopping business, which represents about 20% of Shift4 revenues. 

Beyond the European retail woes, inflation-fatigued Americans are also dining out less. Restaurant sales not only haven’t improved in the second half of 2026, as the company had expected, some comparisons turned negative in October relative to last year, Chief Financial Officer Christopher Cruz said.

Given the conditions, Shift4 has adopted “a conservatism in the way we're looking at the variety of challenges this year” for its financial modeling, as the overall operating environment makes it “hard not to be influenced towards a more cautious approach,” Cruz said in response to an analyst’s question about factors affecting Shift4’s views of 2027.

Shift4 also announced its purchase of Paramount Commerce, a Toronto-based pay-by-bank firm. Terms of the deal, expected to close in the next few weeks, were not disclosed. Paramount enables pay-by-bank deposits and payouts in Canada for companies that include the sports betting sites DraftKings and FanDuel, and Canadian telecommunications firm Telus, Shift4 said in its Thursday third-quarter earnings presentation.

“Bank rails carry the lion’s share of payment volumes in many markets, and account-to-account fits transactions where cards run into limits,” Lauber said on a conference call Thursday with analysts. “This is a kind of normal-course, tuck-in (purchase) that fits right into the Shift4 playbook.”

One issue troubling investors is that Shift4 has failed to articulate a long-term strategy, “especially around Global Blue,” William Blair analyst Andrew Jeffrey wrote last month in a report for the investment firm’s clients. 

The acquisition occurred under former CEO Jared Isaacman, who left the company last year when he was confirmed as administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.

“Our sense is that investors still don’t have a good sense of why this deal happened, whether it was the former CEO’s passion project or it simply reflected a desire for scale,” Jeffrey wrote Oct. 20. Shift4 has “substantial cross-sell potential” with Global Blue among its smaller and medium sized business customers, but hasn’t yet demonstrated it can monetize a new POS device it rolled out to 15 European countries this year.

In a note Thursday, Jeffrey further suggested that Shift4 has relied on a dated model of buying independent software vendors and small acquirers at attractive prices, replacing legacy software systems, and monetizing the technology. 

“This strategy was successful when Shift4 was much smaller, money was free, the merchant processing industry was less competitive, and Shift4 had a knowledge advantage,” he wrote. “Those circumstances no longer exist, in our opinion.”

Shift4 shares have lost about 36% over the past year, including a 4.5% drop on Thursday.

“The share price has clearly not reflected the durability, diversity, and outright caliber of our business and the optimism we feel inside the company,” the CEO said, noting in his remarks that Shift4’s employees, management and founder own about 42% of the company, which is based near Allentown, Pennsylvania. 

Later in the call, Lauber said that “market sentiment in both our business and the broader sector is one that is not rewarding much and is punishing any misgivings.”

title: Hyundai Card’s Alphabet Sub-Brand Tops 150,000 Cards in Three Months
snippet: South Korea's Hyundai Card says its lifestyle-focused Alphabet Card sub-brand, stripped of corporate logos, issued 150,000 cards in its first quarter. The post Hyundai Card’s Alphabet Sub-Brand Tops 150,000 Cards in Three Months appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Hyundai Card issued more than 150,000 cards under its new Alphabet Card sub-brand in the three months following its July 2026 launch, the South Korean financial services company has reported. The figure represents one of the more closely watched early-stage metrics for a branding strategy that deliberately distances the product from the parent company’s identity.

Alphabet Card is built around a category-specific benefits structure in which each letter of the alphabet maps to a spending vertical. Card B covers beauty; Card T covers travel; and so on across a range that includes digital subscriptions and dining. The headline benefit across the range is a 10% discount within the designated category, a deliberately simple proposition designed to reduce the friction of product selection that has long characterised the credit card market.

A brand stripped of its parent

The defining design decision was the removal of the Hyundai Card corporate logo from the front of the physical cards. Hyundai Card also commissioned a custom typeface and bespoke packaging for the range, creating what it describes as an independent brand identity. That choice is significant: it signals an intention to compete on lifestyle resonance rather than the parent group’s name recognition, and it marks Alphabet Card as a product intended to sit alongside, rather than replace, the existing Hyundai Card M and Hyundai Card ZERO general-purpose lines.

A Hyundai Card spokesperson said the product reflects the company’s view that a credit card can function as an expression of personal taste rather than purely a financial utility. “Alphabet Card represents our effort to rethink not only credit card benefits but also the entire brand experience in response to increasingly diverse consumer lifestyles,” the spokesperson said. “Together, these general-purpose and specialised cards complement each other, further expanding Hyundai Card’s product portfolio.”

Market context and competitive read

The South Korean credit card market is mature and competitive, with issuers including Shinhan Card, Samsung Card and KB Kookmin Card all competing for wallet share among digitally fluent consumers. Hyundai Card’s approach borrows from a logic already visible in the co-brand and private label market: that consumers with strong affinity for a specific category are better acquired and retained through a product that speaks directly to that category, rather than a points-accumulation structure that requires active management.

The complementary card positioning is also commercially rational. By targeting existing cardholders who want enhanced returns on a specific vertical, Hyundai Card reduces acquisition cost while lifting spending volume per customer. The risk is cannibalisation of its own general-purpose product economics, though the 10% category discount is narrow enough that a single-card household would likely forgo meaningful breadth of reward.

Beyond its domestic credit card business, Hyundai Card has been expanding into adjacent technology and infrastructure plays. It holds an exclusive Apple Pay partnership in South Korea, issues American Express Centurion card designs as the sole domestic licensee, and in October 2024 signed a contract to supply its proprietary AI platform, UNIVERSE, to Sumitomo Mitsui Card Company in Japan. It is also exploring blockchain-based cross-border payments, a segment drawing increasing regulatory and commercial interest across the Asia-Pacific region.

fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

Read our findings.

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags
snippet: Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests. A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest. Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research. Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. title: The not-so-fine print: making consumer contracts fair
snippet: How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders. When we take action We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use. Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to: Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; andIn some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA. Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress. Examples of cases we've tackledA crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.What we expect of firmsFirms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice. In practice, that means:Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to. Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to usConcerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

How many of us read the terms and conditions of a contract before buying a financial product?

Contracts hold the detail that shapes everyone's financial life, whether you're taking out a loan, insuring your holiday, or signing up for a crypto wallet.

All firms are responsible for making sure that terms in their consumer contracts comply with the fairness and transparency requirements of the Consumer Rights Act (CRA) 2015. When those terms don’t comply, our Consumer Contracts team has powers to challenge firms directly.

This work shows how we use the full range of powers Parliament has given us, not only those in financial services legislation, to tackle harm.

Here's why it matters: if a term is found to be unfair, it's not just unenforceable – consumers may be due redress too. That's why it pays for firms to get this right from the start.

We review contract terms identified through our supervision of firms, information on social media, and referrals from consumers and other external stakeholders.  

When we take action  

We consider our rules and guidance, including the Consumer Duty, when deciding whether to act and which of our regulatory tools to use.  

Where we raise concerns about the fairness or transparency of terms, we expect firms to:  

Amend or delete the relevant terms so that the contract is fair and transparent, and stop relying on those terms in existing contracts.

Pay redress to consumers if the firm’s use of the terms has caused harm; and

In some cases, give us a voluntary undertaking under the CRA.  

Where necessary, we can apply for a court injunction to prevent a firm from using or enforcing the term against its customers. We can also seek a court order requiring it to pay redress.  

Examples of cases we've tackled

A crypto firm agreed to stop charging excessive storage fees which, in some cases, could exceed £40,000 a year. We intervened after finding it had charged inactive customers a disproportionate amount. The firm removed the term and paid redress to affected consumers.

A financial adviser updated its contracts after trying to charge a customer £800 for time spent handling a complaint. The charge was included in its terms and conditions, but we considered the term unfair because it could put people off making legitimate complaints. We also considered it inconsistent with the Consumer Duty and our own rules.

A travel insurer clarified unclear terms about what counted as a 12-hour delay and paid out £18,000 in redress to customers whose claims had been wrongly denied. Here, ambiguous wording was the problem, so we pushed for clearer terms that told consumers exactly what they were entitled to.

A lender improved the terms of a new credit product to give clearer information on costs and cancellation rights after we raised concerns ahead of launch. This is a good example of intervening early, through the authorisations process, to prevent unfair terms making it to market in the first place.

What we expect of firms

Firms should regularly check that their consumer contracts are fair, clear and transparent, and that they're being used fairly in practice.  

In practice, that means:

Taking into account consumers’ legitimate interests when designing contracts.

Using plain language, so customers understand what they're agreeing to: for example, what they might have to pay and what rights they have. Nobody should need a law degree to understand what they're signing up to.  

Avoiding surprises, by making important terms – fees, cancellation rights, variations, exclusions, complaints – easy to spot.

Reviewing contracts regularly to stay compliant with the latest requirements, rulings and judgments, and to learn from complaints, claims, cancellations, fees, customer outcomes and other data.

Testing whether customers actually understand key terms – not just assuming they do.

Improving staff training to ensure staff meet the standards set out in product literature, including contracts. Using complaints data to identify potentially unfair or unclear contract terms and make appropriate changes.

How to report concerns about unfair or unclear terms to us

Concerned about an unfair or unclear term in a financial services firm’s consumer contract? You can report it to us using our form. We can't always tell you what action we've taken, but, we can assure you, every report we receive gets considered.

title: Block to provide data to FTC
snippet: The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

The company said it will turn over documents the Federal Trade Commission sought in January in response to a probe of complaints about Square.

        

            

        Published Nov. 10, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                The Federal Trade Commission offices on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington DC.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Block will comply with a Federal Trade Commission request for information as part of a regulatory inquiry into some 1,500 merchant complaints alleging the company froze or deactivated Square user accounts without notice. Block said in a court filing Friday that it would produce the materials the agency sought in three batches by year-end.

“For the sake of efficiency and to avoid the burden and delay of litigation, the parties now wish to resolve the issues in the Petition, and all other issues related to compliance with” the FTC’s civil investigative demand, attorneys for Block and the FTC said in a joint filing to the federal court. Block said it “disputes and does not admit the allegations” in the agency’s petition.

The FTC argued in a court filing last month that Block had not complied with its Jan. 22 civil investigative demand, despite several meetings between attorneys for the parties. The agency asked U.S. Magistrate Judge Sallie Kim to enforce its investigative demand.

Dive Insight:

Besides the Square point-of-sale business, Block owns Cash App and Afterpay, a buy now, pay later service. The Oakland, California-based company was founded and is led by Jack Dorsey, who also founded the social media company Twitter.

The Square user complaints at issue “allege that Block has wrongfully withheld at least $2.5 million of Square users’ payment proceeds since 2022,” the FTC said in its Oct. 7 filing with the U.S. District Court in San Francisco. “Given the FTC’s experience that only a small fraction of injured consumers complain to the government, these losses may be just the tip of the iceberg,” the regulator said.

Spokespeople for the FTC and Block declined to comment Monday on the filing or about which time period the alleged Square complaints cover.

Block agreed to respond to 47 interrogatories the FTC has posed about the Square matter and produce all non-privileged documents and non-privileged portions of partially privileged documents by Nov. 13, according to the joint filing. Block also will make a second submission to the FTC of additional information by Nov. 30. By year-end, Block also will turn over “all responsive non-privileged documents with one or more search term hits” detailed in an email last month between the parties, the filing said.

The request contained 47 questions, 21 documents requests and four separate data requests, according to the FTC’s October filing for the court’s intervention.

The FTC’s attorneys said its January demand gave Block until Feb. 18 to seek to quash or modify the agency’s request, “but Block never filed a petition to quash or modify the CID (demand), nor sought any extension of time to file the petition.”

Block’s attorneys with Gibson Dunn & Crutcher also asked the court Friday to seal some “confidential information that would cause Block particularized business harm if it were disclosed publicly.” The request pertains to Block presentations to directors and senior executives about its fraud-prevention and risk-management efforts, the company said.

The investigative demand is the third by a government agency against Block since 2021, the FTC noted in its petition to the court, citing court requests by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the Washington state attorney general.

title: California takes CoinFlip to task
snippet: The state ordered the crypto ATM company to pay $4.8 million to scam victims, and bashed federal regulators over failing to police for fraud.
fullText:
California regulators demanded this week that crypto ATM operator CoinFlip pay scam victims $4.8 million in restitution for fraud that took place at the company’s machines in the state.

The state’s new Business and Consumer Services Agency, tasked with protecting consumers from financial fraud, issued a notice Thursday saying CoinFlip had violated state and federal laws by not better protecting its customers from fraud that was perpetrated through the company’s machines that exchange cash for crypto.

“An investigation by California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation found that, over the past five years, CoinFlip failed to detect, prevent, report, and mitigate suspicious activity, paving the way for scammers to exploit Californians and steal their hard–earned money,” the California agency said in the release.

The regulators noted that some of the laws that were breached by CoinFlip are expressly to protect Californians using crypto kiosks.

CoinFlip didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

CoinFlip, which is based in Chicago and was founded in 2015, says on its website that it is the world’s “largest network of cryptocurrency ATMs by transaction volume.” It offers services at some 5,500 bitcoin ATMs in six countries, including 48 states in the U.S., according to the website. About 500 of the company’s crypto kiosks exist in California, typically at grocery and convenience stores or gas stations, according to the state agency. 

Crypto fraud is an expanding part of schemes that target the elderly, including in scams where criminals lure consumers to provide funds under false pretenses, sometimes asking them to transfer money.

“Because transactions are immediate, hard to track, and cannot be reversed, crypto ATMs like those in CoinFlip's network have become the tool of choice for fraudsters looking to exploit consumers — especially older Americans,” the California release said.

California’s Business and Consumer Services Agency was conceived last year as part of a restructuring of state agencies by Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat. The revised government structure was finalized in July of this year.

The action against CoinFlip “is the latest example of our work to ensure new technology actually helps people, rather than driving up prices or opening the doors to fraud — a key priority of California's consumer watchdog agency,” the release said.

Rohit Chopra was appointed in May to lead the new California agency. He formerly headed the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau during President Joe Biden’s administration, and left the CFPB post last year after President Donald Trump became president. Chopra also was Commissioner at the Federal Trade Commission until 2021 during Trump’s first administration.

With the start of the second Trump Administration, the CFPB’s workforce was chopped and the president’s leadership expressed an interest in shuttering the agency. The agency has since reversed course on policies that were put in place by Chopra, including with respect to emerging digital financial service offerings.

Chopra took a swipe at the Trump administration polices in the release announcing the state’s action against CoinFlip. His comments landed in a week in which Democrats broadly won elections nationwide, both at the federal and state levels. Newsom has widely been seen as a potential 2028 presidential candidate.

“As federal regulators give a free pass to crimes against consumers, California continues to chart a different path. While consumers can no longer rely on federal regulators to protect them, we are doubling down to ensure that new technology does not turbocharge fraud and that bad actors are held accountable,” the release said.

title: Will a ‘blue wave’ push the CCCA?
snippet: With Sen. Roger Marshall voted out and Sen. Dick Durbin retiring, the Credit Card Competition Act faces an uncertain future.
fullText:
The ‘blue wave’ of Democrat victories in Congress this week washed Republican Sen. Roger Marshall out of office, tapering his support for the Credit Card Competition Act.

Sen. Dick Durbin, the Democrat who has been his partner in the push to pass that bill aimed at lowering card swipe fees for merchants, has already said he’s retiring at the end of this term.

That means that at the start of a new Congress next year, the bill won’t have its two biggest co-sponsors of the past few years in the Senate. That could make a meaningful difference for a piece of legislation that has struggled to win passage since Durbin and Marshall first introduced the legislation in 2022.

The bill, which takes aim at Visa and Mastercard, would force banks that issue credit cards to ensure that an alternative card network, other than those two dominant players, was available to process a transaction. The idea is to create more competition in the card network market in a bid to lower fees that merchants are charged for processing cards.

CCCA proponent Doug Kantor, who has long worked on behalf of merchants as general counsel for the National Association of Convenience Stores, called it “painful” to lose Marshall’s support of the legislation. 

But Kantor noted in an interview Wednesday that Marshall has helped win more support of the bill in this congressional session, including from President Donald Trump. Kantor counted nine times that Trump or Vice President JD Vance, a former Senate sponsor of the bill, have publicly called for passage of the legislation. Albeit, much of that public promotion came as part of their failed efforts to see Marshall reelected.

Backers of the bill could still seek to advance it in the final two months of this year, before the two-year congressional session ends and the newly elected senators and representatives arrive, but Kantor didn’t seem hopeful. 

He said it depends on how productive the senators and representatives decide to be when they return to Washington. There are still some spending bills that will move this year and they could be vehicles for carrying the bill across the finish line.

The bill has “as good a shot as many other things to move,” offered Kantor, who also sits on the executive committee of the Merchants Payments Coalition.

However, with so many senators and representatives headed for an exit, and a Thanksgiving Day respite from campaigning just a few weeks away, it’s easy to see them coasting toward the year-end break. 

When asked about future support for the bill, a spokesperson for Durbin pointed to Sen. Peter Welch, a Democrat from Vermont who has been a Senate sponsor of the legislation, and was also in his prior role as a House representative. Durbin this month handed the torch to Welch, according to a report from the political publication PunchBowl News.

The bill benefited from having a Republican leaning in alongside a Democrat, with Marshall throwing his weight behind Durbin’s longtime fight against the top credit card networks. The legislation also had bipartisan backing in the House, where Republican Rep. Lance Good of Texas and Democratic Rep. Zoe Lofgren of California have supported the bill. Both hung onto their seats. 

As far as finding a new Senate Republican to champion the bill, Kantor suggested the existing sponsors would fill that need. With Sen. Cynthia Lummis retiring, that would seem to leave only Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio, a state that just returned Democrat Sherrod Brown to the chamber in the latest election.

Opponents of the bill have no doubt that the merchant advocates of the legislation will keep up their years-long campaign to pass the bill. The Electronic Payments Coalition is one of the groups that has battled the bill. They’re bracing for the ongoing clash.

“Our work will continue to focus on educating Americans and policymakers about the real-world consequences of proposed credit card legislation, including its potential impact on small business and consumer access to credit, community financial institutions, data security protections, and cash back and other rewards programs,” EPC Executive Chairman Richard Hunt told members of that group in an emailed note Wednesday morning.

Hunt noted CCCA proponents, including at the National Restaurant Association, are casting the legislation as an “affordability” issue, a theme that helped Democrats win seats across the country. Backers of the bill argue that merchants paying higher fees means prices go up for consumers.

If that becomes the central thrust, there’s always the possibility that the new Congress moves right past paying attention to card fees paid by merchants, and focuses instead on interest rates paid by card holding consumers. 

That might play into the hands of Sens. Bernie Sanders, an Independent from Vermont, and Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, who will remain in the next Congress. Last year, they introduced a bill to cap card interest rates at 10% and will presumably keep pushing for passage.

It’s a bill that has also won backing from Trump and might have improved chances with more Democrats on Capitol Hill.
